Then I’m sitting there staring at the screen, and meanwhile the ticket’s still open. She says my grade school report cards always had that line, you know, “bright kid, but…” and then it was that I wouldn’t stay in my seat, I’d blurt out answers, and I’d lose homework even when I’d actually done it.\n\nI remember some of that, but mostly I remember her being frustrated because she knew I’d done the work and then somehow it just never made it into the teacher’s hands. It’s funny, because she still says it like it was cute, but at the time I don’t think it felt cute.\n\nDoctor: Outside of work, does this same attention problem also cause trouble in other parts of your life?\n\nPatient: Yeah, it does. It’s not just work-work, if that makes sense. When I had the old job, there was more structure around me, and I didn’t realize how much I was leaning on that. Since that went away, things have gotten… messier.\n\nI tried doing freelance support stuff, and I’d mean to follow through, but then I’d miss something or take too long getting back to people, and clients just stopped calling. And in this field people talk, you know? Your name either means “reliable” or it doesn’t. Mine has taken a hit.\n\nThere was also a senior service-manager role I thought I had a real shot at, and I missed out on it. I keep thinking if I’d been more on top of things, maybe that goes differently. And then at home, my wife and I are looking at bills and it’s like… this isn’t just me being scattered. It’s affecting money. It’s affecting whether people trust me to do what I say I’m going to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?\n\nPatient: I mean… I worry about things, sure. But “a lot about many different things,” I’m not totally sure how to answer that.\n\nSometimes it’s more like one thing grabs me and I keep circling it, and then I’ll get distracted by something else entirely—like I’ll be thinking about a bill and suddenly I’m remembering I never replied to someone about a router issue. So… I don’t know if that counts as worrying, exactly, or just my mind bouncing around.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it depressed most days. I mean, I get discouraged, especially when I’m behind on things or I feel like I’ve dropped the ball again. But “down most days” sounds more… constant, I guess?\n\nSome days I’m fine, or at least I’m busy enough that I don’t think about it. Then something reminds me—like an email I meant to answer, or my wife asking about something I forgot—and I feel lousy for a while. Even when I’m supposed to just sit still and listen, it’s like there’s this motor humming under my skin.\n\nLike I’ll be in a chair and part of me is already thinking I should stand up, go check something, fix something, move on to the next problem right now. It’s not always that I actually need to do anything, it just feels… urgent, I guess. Like sitting still is wasting time, even if I’m supposed to be paying attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you use any substances or medications that seem to make your concentration worse?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’ve noticed anything specific like, “Oh, when I take this or use that, my concentration gets worse.”\n\nI guess sometimes if I’m tired or I’ve had too much coffee or whatever, I can feel more scattered, but I don’t know if that’s a substance thing or just… me. And with work, I’m around computers all day, and honestly half the time the thing that ruins my concentration is somebody calling about a password reset while I’m in the middle of something else.\n\nBut, um… no, I can’t point to a medication or substance that clearly makes it worse.\n\nDoctor: Have these attention problems caused significant trouble in more than one area of your life, such as both work and home?\n\nPatient: Yeah, definitely more than one area. Work is the obvious one, but it’s not just work.\n\nSince I lost the structure of my old job, things have kind of… come apart. My reputation took a hit. I’ve lost freelance clients because I didn’t follow through the way I should have, and there was this senior service-manager role I really thought I had a shot at, but I missed out on that too.\n\nAnd then it follows me home, because my wife and I end up worrying about money, and it’s not just the money, it’s that people don’t trust me to do what I say I’m going to do. That’s a hard thing to sit with.\n\nDoctor: Did these concentration problems get much worse after a particular stressful life event?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I think it really got bad after I was fired. Not that I was perfect before, but after that, I lost all the structure that used to keep me moving in the right direction.\n\nIt’s been… about a year and ten months now, I guess. But then I’ll get sidetracked thinking about the practical stuff, like which email I forgot to answer or whether I should redo my resume again, and then I’m not even sure if I’m describing stress or just the mess around it.\n\nSo… I guess I can’t say for sure. I know things got harder after the job loss, but I don’t have a neat answer about whether it was specifically more stress than usual.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure. I haven’t really noticed it in that clear way.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself unable to stop or control your worrying?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it worrying exactly. I haven’t really noticed it in that clear way. Or I forget to pay the cloud backup bill, which is embarrassing because I’m supposed to be the computer guy, you know? And then there was a volunteer class where I brought the wrong adapter, or didn’t bring the right one, and the whole thing got delayed.

Then I spend the next day apologizing, explaining, trying to patch over whatever I messed up. It’s exhausting, and it makes me look careless even when I really did intend to do it.

It’s affecting whether people trust me to do what I say I’m going to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?\n\nPatient: I mean… I worry about things, sure. Bills, work, whether I’m messing something up—normal stuff, I guess. But “a lot about many different things,” I’m not totally sure how to answer that.\n\nSometimes it’s more like one thing grabs me and I keep circling it, and then I’ll get distracted by something else entirely—like I’ll be thinking about a bill and suddenly I’m remembering I never replied to someone about a router issue. So… I don’t know if that counts as worrying, exactly, or just my mind bouncing around.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it depressed most days. I mean, I get discouraged, especially when I’m behind on things or I feel like I’ve dropped the ball again. But “down most days” sounds more… constant, I guess?\n\nSome days I’m fine, or at least I’m busy enough that I don’t think about it. Then something reminds me—like an email I meant to answer, or my wife asking about something I forgot—and I feel lousy for a while. But I’m not sure if that’s depression or just being frustrated with myself.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel restless, like you have a hard time sitting still?\n\nPatient: Yeah. Restless is probably the right word. Even when I’m supposed to just sit still and listen, it’s like there’s this motor humming under my skin.\n\nLike I’ll be in a chair and part of me is already thinking I should stand up, go check something, fix something, move on to the next problem right now. It’s not always that I actually need to do anything, it just feels… urgent, I guess. Like sitting still is wasting time, even if I’m supposed to be paying attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you use any substances or medications that seem to make your concentration worse?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’ve noticed anything specific like, “Oh, when I take this or use that, my concentration gets worse.”\n\nI guess sometimes if I’m tired or I’ve had too much coffee or whatever, I can feel more scattered, but I don’t know if that’s a substance thing or just… me. And with work, I’m around computers all day, and honestly half the time the thing that ruins my concentration is somebody calling about a password reset while I’m in the middle of something else.\n\nBut, um… no, I can’t point to a medication or substance that clearly makes it worse.\n\nDoctor: Have these attention problems caused significant trouble in more than one area of your life, such as both work and home?\n\nPatient: Yeah, definitely more than one area. Work is the obvious one, but it’s not just work.\n\nSince I lost the structure of my old job, things have kind of… come apart. My reputation took a hit. I’ve lost freelance clients because I didn’t follow through the way I should have, and there was this senior service-manager role I really thought I had a shot at, but I missed out on that too.\n\nAnd then it follows me home, because my wife and I end up worrying about money, and it’s not just the money, it’s that people don’t trust me to do what I say I’m going to do. That’s a hard thing to sit with.\n\nDoctor: Did these concentration problems get much worse after a particular stressful life event?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I think it really got bad after I was fired. Not that I was perfect before, but after that, I lost all the structure that used to keep me moving in the right direction.\n\nIt’s been… about a year and ten months now, I guess. Funny how I can remember that, even though I’ll forget something I was supposed to send five minutes later. But yeah, since losing that job and the systems around it, it’s been causing real trouble.\n\nDoctor: Before you were fired, were these attention problems already causing serious trouble at work?\n\nPatient: Before I was fired… I mean, there were problems, but the really serious trouble has been since then. Once I lost that job and all the systems that kind of kept me on track, that’s when things really started falling apart.\n\nSo I’d say it’s been about a year and ten months of it causing serious trouble. Before that, I could sort of get by more, even if it wasn’t perfect.\n\nDoctor: Since losing that job, have you been feeling noticeably more stressed than usual?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, losing the job was stressful, obviously, but “noticeably more stressed than usual”... I don’t know. My usual has kind of shifted, if that makes sense.\n\nSome days I think, yes, I must be more stressed, because everything feels more loaded. But then I’ll get sidetracked thinking about the practical stuff, like which email I forgot to answer or whether I should redo my resume again, and then I’m not even sure if I’m describing stress or just the mess around it.\n\nSo… I guess I can’t say for sure. I know things got harder after the job loss, but I don’t have a neat answer about whether it was specifically more stress than usual.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure. I mean, I still like the things I like, I think. It’s just hard to tell sometimes because I’ll start doing something and then get pulled off into something else, or I’ll think, “Oh, I should relax,” and then I spend 40 minutes messing with settings on the TV or checking some random thing online.\n\nSo… I don’t know if I’ve lost interest exactly. I haven’t really noticed it in that clear way.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself unable to stop or control your worrying?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it worrying exactly. I mean, I do get stuck on things sometimes, like I’ll be thinking about one thing and then it turns into three other things, and suddenly I’m looking up something totally different or trying to remember if I handled some random task.\n\nBut “unable to stop or control worrying”… I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed it in that clear way. Maybe I’d need you to say what you mean by worrying.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have trouble getting organized for tasks, like keeping track of steps, deadlines, or what needs to be done first?\n\nPatient: Yes. That one I can answer pretty clearly. Without the old ticketing system and the escalation calendar from work, my day just kind of turns into… piles.\n\nI’ll have sticky notes, half-written emails, reminders for chess club stuff, parts orders I meant to follow up on, and then I’ll look at all of it and honestly not know what has to happen first. I’ll think, okay, I should answer this email, but then I remember a part number, and then I’m checking something else, and then suddenly the thing with the actual deadline is already overdue.\n\nSo yes, keeping the steps and priorities straight is a real problem.\n\nDoctor: Do these attention problems make it hard for you to finish tasks even when you understand exactly what needs to be done?\n\nPatient: Yes. That’s actually probably the main reason I’m here.\n\nI can understand the task perfectly, like if I’m tracing a client’s network issue, I know what I’m supposed to check and in what order. But then ten minutes later I realize I’ve been staring at the same log entries, or rereading the same lines three times, and I still couldn’t tell you what they say.\n\nAnd then sometimes I’ll click over to check one related thing, and that reminds me of another thing, and—sorry, this is how it goes—I’m suddenly not even on the original problem anymore. But yes, even when I know exactly what needs doing, keeping my mind on it long enough to finish is really hard.\n\nDoctor: When you lose focus on a task, is it usually because your attention gets pulled to something unrelated rather than because you’re stuck worrying about the task?\n\nPatient: Yeah, usually it’s not that I’m sitting there worrying about the task. It’s more like something yanks my attention away.\n\nIf I’m working from home and the dishwasher clicks, or somebody walks past the window, or I suddenly think, “Oh, I should fix that other machine,” then I’m just… gone. I’ll be off the original job before I even realize I left it. I’ve lost freelance clients because I didn’t keep on top of things, and there was a senior service-manager role I was hoping for that I missed out on. And then that turns into money stress at home, obviously.\n\nMy wife tries not to say it like that, but I can tell she’s worried, and I don’t blame her. It’s hard on a marriage when your spouse can’t count on you to do the things you said you’d do.\n\nDoctor: Do you often forget everyday obligations, like appointments, paying bills, or returning calls?\n\nPatient: Yes, all the time. It’s exhausting, and it makes me look careless even when I really did intend to do it.\n\nDoctor: Do you often put off or avoid tasks that require sustained mental effort?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure how to answer that.
